title: Kenya Boosts Power Imports as Rising Demand Puts Grid Under Pressure
desc: Kenya increased electricity imports from Ethiopia and Uganda as rising demand put pressure on local generation and raised concerns over power rationing.
content:
Kenya is increasingly relying on electricity imports from neighbouring countries as rising demand continues to put pressure on the national power grid.

New data for the six months to June 2026 shows that imported electricity accounted for 12 per cent of the power supplied to Kenya Power, up from 10 per cent during the same period last year. Ethiopia remained the main source of the additional imported supply, while imports from Uganda also increased.

The growing dependence highlights a challenge facing Kenya's energy sector: electricity demand from homes and businesses is rising faster than the available cushion in local generation capacity.

For ordinary consumers, the issue matters because a tight electricity reserve can increase the risk of supply interruptions, particularly during periods of high demand. Businesses can also face disruption when unreliable power affects operations, production and operating costs.

Kenya Power has previously warned that dependence on imported hydropower carries risks of its own. A serious drought or other disruption in neighbouring countries could affect their ability to maintain electricity exports to Kenya.

The pressure on the grid has also been reflected in concerns over the country's shrinking reserve margin. Recent reporting showed that the gap between available electricity capacity and demand had narrowed, increasing concerns about possible power cuts if supply comes under further strain.

Imported electricity is helping Kenya meet current demand, but the trend raises wider questions about long-term energy security.

A growing economy requires reliable electricity for households, factories, hospitals, schools and small businesses. While regional power trading can provide an important backup, Kenya's long-term stability will also depend on expanding and strengthening domestic generation.

The increase in imports therefore tells two sides of the same story.

On one hand, regional connections with countries such as Ethiopia and Uganda are helping Kenya keep electricity flowing when local supply is under pressure. On the other, the growing reliance exposes how narrow the country's electricity reserve has become.

For consumers, the most important question is whether Kenya can maintain reliable power while demand continues to rise.

The answer will depend on how quickly new local generation comes online and whether the country can strengthen its grid before supply pressure turns into more widespread electricity interruptions.
